records.quote:
"To be or not to be" was the telephone number of the municipal gas
chambers of the Federal Bureau of Termination.
records.paraphrase: A government agency operates gas chambers accessible by phone number.

records.quote:
He knew that he would never paint again. He let his paintbrush fall to
the dropcloths below.
records.paraphrase: The painter is so affected he decides to stop painting.

records.quote:
The painter pondered the mournful puzzle of life demanding to be born
and, once born, demanding to be fruitful ... to multiply and to live as
long as possible--to do all that on a very small planet that would have
to last forever.
records.paraphrase: The painter reflects on the fundamental problem of unlimited life on a finite planet.

records.quote:
And then he decided he had had about enough of
life in the Happy Garden of Life, too
records.paraphrase: The painter decides he is done with living.

records.quote: Death, barring accidents, was an adventure for volunteers.
records.paraphrase: Because aging is cured, death only comes to those who volunteer for it.

records.quote:
Without population
control, human beings would now be packed on this surface of this old
planet like drupelets on a blackberry!
records.paraphrase: Hitz explains that population control prevents catastrophic overcrowding.

records.quote:
The law said that no newborn child could survive unless the parents of
the child could find someone who would volunteer to die.
records.paraphrase: Law requires a volunteer death for each newborn to be allowed to live.

records.quote: X-rays had revealed that his wife was going to have triplets.
records.paraphrase: X-ray imaging revealed triplets before birth.

records.quote:
Aging had
touched him that much before the cure for aging was found.
records.paraphrase: A cure for aging was discovered at a certain point.

records.quote:
There were no prisons, no slums, no insane asylums, no cripples, no
poverty, no wars.
records.paraphrase: The society has eliminated prisons, poverty, and war.

records.quote:
The population of the United States was stabilized at forty-million
souls.
records.paraphrase: The national population is held fixed at forty million.

records.quote: "I want those kids," said Wehling quietly. "I want all three of them."
records.paraphrase: Wehling expresses that he wants all three of his newborn children.

records.quote: And then he shot himself, making room for all three of his children.
records.paraphrase: Wehling kills himself and two others so all three children can live.

records.quote:
In the year 2000," said Dr. Hitz, "before scientists stepped in and
laid down the law, there wasn't even enough drinking water to go around,
and nothing to eat but sea-weed
records.paraphrase: Prior overpopulation led to shortages of water and food until scientists intervened.

records.quote:
All the answers that the painter could think of were grim. Even grimmer,
surely, than a Catbox, a Happy Hooligan, an Easy Go. He thought of war.
He thought of plague. He thought of starvation.
records.paraphrase: The painter concludes alternatives to termination are worse: war, plague, starvation.

records.quote:
Two centuries ago, when I was a young man,
it was a hell that nobody thought could last another twenty years. Now
centuries of peace and plenty stretch before us as far as the
imagination cares to travel.
records.paraphrase: Hitz contrasts the past hellish crowded world with the present peaceful plenty.

records.quote: All diseases were conquered. So was old age.
records.paraphrase: Disease and aging have been cured.

records.quote:
Would you like to go back to the good old days, when the population of
the Earth was twenty billion--about to become forty billion, then eighty
billion, then one hundred and sixty billion?
records.paraphrase: Hitz describes runaway population growth that justified the new controls.

records.quote:
Wehling shot Dr. Hitz dead. "There's room for one--a great big one," he
said.
records.paraphrase: Wehling murders Dr. Hitz to make room for a child.

records.quote:
Wehling was fifty-six, a mere stripling in a population whose average
age was one hundred and twenty-nine.
records.paraphrase: The average lifespan is now around 129, making a 56-year-old young.

quarantined.reason: quote could not be located in prepared story

candidate.quote:
A curious thing about gas-chamber hostesses was that, no matter how lovely
and feminine they were when recruited, they all sprouted mustaches
within five years or so.
candidate.paraphrase: Gas-chamber hostesses reportedly grow mustaches after years of the work.

criteria.rationale: The cure for aging and conquest of all disease are speculative biomedical sciences central to the premise; X-rays and demographic science (drupelet packing) also feature.

The Federal Bureau of Termination's municipal gas chambers are an engineered institutional system that materially drives the setting, problem, and outcome (Wehling's crisis, the painter's final call).
The story is set in a speculative future where average age is 129 and events reference the year 2000 as a distant past relative to the two-centuries-later present.

The narrative systematically develops the consequences of curing aging on a finite planet: mandatory population control, one-death-per-birth law, and the grim social calculus the painter contemplates.

There is reference to scientists stepping in and reasoning about population, and the painter reflectively reasons about the puzzle, but no observation/hypothesis/testing cycle materially drives the action; the inference is contemplative rather than methodical.
The story is set entirely on Earth with no other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors; 'planet' references are to Earth itself.

The averted large-scale catastrophe of runaway overpopulation (twenty billion, water/food shortages, remembered war/plague/starvation) is causally central to the world; the shootings are personal-scale rather than the mass catastrophe.

candidates.description: A society in which aging and disease have been cured, granting effective immortality, coupled with a legal population-control regime that fixes the population and requires a volunteer death (via state Ethical Suicide Studios) for every newborn permitted to live.

novelty.rationale: The conquest of aging and disease combined with a mandatory death-for-birth law is a totalizing departure from the empirical norm: it restructures mortality, demography, law, and social institutions across the entire storyworld, not merely a local gadget.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The story supplies a coherent, immanent, nonsupernatural rationale: unchecked immortality plus reproduction on a finite planet caused catastrophic overpopulation, so scientists imposed a systematic population-control law with an institutional apparatus (Federal Bureau of Termination). The logic is internally consistent social-scientific extrapolation, satisfying cognitive validation regardless of engineering detail.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The entire plot is generated by this novum: Wehling's dilemma over his triplets, the murders, and the painter's suicide all follow directly from the death-for-birth law and immortality regime. It governs the overriding narrative logic rather than being incidental.

estrangement.rationale: The reader is estranged by the contrast between a euphemistic utopia ('Happy Garden of Life,' 'Ethical Suicide Studios') and the horror of state-mandated death, dramatized by Wehling's murders and the painter's final call to be terminated.

candidates.description: The Federal Bureau of Termination and its municipal gas chambers ('Ethical Suicide Studios'), a state institution reachable by the phone number 2BR02B that euthanizes volunteers.

novelty.rationale: A normalized state euthanasia institution accessible by telephone is a departure from the empirical norm, but it is an institutional expression of the broader immortality/population-control novum rather than an independent world-altering difference.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The institution follows coherently and immanently from the population-control logic; it is a plausible bureaucratic apparatus within the story's own systematic account.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The Bureau frames the story (title, ending call) but it functions as a subordinate mechanism of the death-for-birth law; the driving narrative logic is the underlying immortality/population regime, not the Bureau as a standalone device.

estrangement.rationale: The euphemistic nicknames ('Catbox,' 'Sheepdip,' 'Ethical Suicide Studios') and the warm hostess thanking the caller on behalf of future generations estrange the reader by dressing mass euthanasia as cheerful public service.
